title: Short Stuff: Suicide Forest
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Aokigahara Forest at the northwest base of Mount Fuji in Japan, also called the "suicide forest" and "Jukai" (sea of trees). Hosts give a content warning, then cover the forest's reputation and the government's decision to stop publishing suicide statistics. They discuss the origins of the reputation: the ascetic Buddhist sokushinbutsu mummification practice, the 1960 short story "Tower of Waves" by Seichō Matsumoto, the 1930s Japanese youth volcano suicides and a 1935 Time article, and the 1993 manual "The Complete Suicide Manual" by Wataru Tsurumi. They describe the prevention signs, staff training, and cameras in the forest, and close with a reminder of the crisis helpline.

segments.title: Opening and trigger warning
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode, note it is a shorty from Dave Bruce, and issue a trigger warning about the Aokigahara Forest, which is nicknamed the suicide forest. They provide the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

segments.title: Aokigahara Forest and its reputation
segments.summary: The forest, also called the Jukai (sea of trees), lies on the flank of Mount Fuji about a couple hours from Tokyo and grew over a lava flow from an 864 eruption. It is known as the suicide forest. The Japanese government stopped publishing suicide counts in the mid-2010s.

segments.title: Sokushinbutsu self-mummification origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the origin of one proposed link: ascetic Buddhist monks who meditated in forests, subsisted on leaves and bark, and buried themselves alive in crypts to mummify, as described in the sokushinbutsu tradition. Scientists think the mummies were prepared after death. Some suggest this practice inspired the forest's reputation, though the hosts doubt it.

segments.title: Tower of Waves and the 1960 story
segments.summary: The hosts describe Seichō Matsumoto's 1960 short story Tower of Waves, a Romeo and Juliet-style tale in which a young woman writes a farewell letter, takes pills, and goes into the forest to die. Many consider it the first literary link between the forest and suicide.

segments.title: Japanese youth volcano suicides and cultural views
segments.summary: The hosts describe 1920s to 1930s mass hysteria in which teenage girls threw themselves into volcanoes, including a girl named Kiyoko who jumped into the active Mount Mihara. They cite a 1935 Time article that covered the phenomenon in a tongue-in-cheek way. They argue Western readers misread Japanese views: modern Japanese culture opposes suicide and works to prevent it, without the same religious morality.

segments.title: Prevention efforts and The Complete Suicide Manual
segments.summary: The hosts note Japan's prevention and crisis hotlines, and staff and volunteer training and security cameras in the forest. They describe the 1993 Japanese-language book The Complete Suicide Manual by Wataru Tsurumi, a step-by-step guide that calls the forest the perfect place to die. Some such manuals have reportedly been found with people who died in the forest.

segments.title: Effects on families and communities
segments.summary: Josh argues that suicide in the forest affects more than the family, as people who find the bodies, volunteers who clean the forest, residents nearby, and police are all affected.

segments.title: Prevention signs in the forest
segments.summary: Signs at the forest entrance urge visitors to think of their parents, siblings and children, to talk about their troubles, and include a suicide helpline number.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Hosts briefly praise the forest's beauty and sign off. Credits note the show is an iHeartRadio production.
